events.name: The Seoul Guardians
events.description: Joie Chen, an Emmy-winning anchor and correspondent formerly of CNN, Al Jazeera, and CBS News will join directors Kim Jong-woo, Kim Shin-wan, and Cho Chul-young for an onstage conversation after the screening. Watch the Trailer On the night of December 3, 2024, then-president Yoon Suk Yeol declared martial law in Korea. He banned all political activities and public assemblies and sent troops to the National Assembly building to seize control. The Seoul Guardians plunges you into the political chaos of that night, with codirecting by three journalists who were there. Lawmakers rush to pass a bill ending martial law as ordinary citizens band together to hold off the soldiers sent to take the building. The winner of multiple film festival awards, this stirring documentary resonates with audiences around the world with its message that democracy is fragile and must be defended. Directors: Kim Jong-woo, Kim Shin-wan, and Cho Chul-young. Country: Korea. Released: 2026. Length: 70 min. Format: DCP. Language: Korean with English subtitles. Image courtesy of Asian Shadows

events.name: Sneak Peek | Saodat Ismailova and Marianne Kamp in Conversation
events.description: Saodat Ismailova’s films weave together archival materials and her own footage to explore Central Asia’s layered histories and landscapes, from the region’s ancient past and Islamic traditions through the Soviet era and into the present. In this online program, Ismailova considers these subjects in conversation with Dr. Marianne Kamp, whose landmark studies of Uzbek social transformation have explored the lives of women and youth amid Soviet-era modernization and unveiling. Together, their reflections invite us to consider how personal memory, oral history, and historical archives can illuminate the political, social, and environmental changes that have shaped Central Asia. Born in Uzbekistan in 1981, Saodat Ismailova is an Uzbek filmmaker and artist living and working between Paris and Tashkent. She graduated from the Tashkent State Art Institute and Le Fresnoy—National Studio of Contemporary Arts in France. In 2021, she initiated Davra, a research collective dedicated to developing the Central Asian art scene. Ismailova participated in both the 59th Venice Biennale and documenta fifteen in 2022. The same year, she received The Eye Art & Film Prize (Amsterdam). In 2025, she received Foundation Pernod Ricard’s Nouveau Programme Award, was named an Art Basel Golden Awardee, and received the Han Nefkens Award for a new commission together with the Reina Sofía Museum (Madrid), Walker Center (USA), and the Singapore Museum of Arts. Her works are included in the collections of Tate Modern, London; Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam; Centre Pompidou, Paris; TBA21; FRAC Corsica; the Victoria and Albert Museum, London; and the Almaty Museum of Arts, Kazakhstan; among others. Marianne Kamp is an associate professor in the Central Eurasian Studies Department at Indiana University. She is a social historian of modern Central Asia who uses oral history methods to explore transformations in everyday life during the Soviet period and since the independence of the “-stans” in 1991. Dr. Kamp is author of Collectivization Generation: Oral Histories of a Social Revolution in Uzbekistan (Cornell 2024), The New Woman in Uzbekistan: Islam, Modernity, and Unveiling under Communism (University of Washington Press 2006); of an edited translation, with Mariana Markova, Muslim Women of the Russian Empire: Vladimir and Maria Nalivkins’ Nineteenth-Century Fergana Valley Ethnography (Indiana University Press, 2016); and of numerous articles and chapters. This program is part of the online lunchtime series Sneak Peek , where staff members and outside scholars share personal perspectives and new research related to the collections of the National Museum of Asian Art. events.name: ONLINE | In Conversation: Emma Alcazar and Nikki Corbett, Moderated by Veruschka Zarate
events.description: Hear from the designers of the second two block patterns in the museum’s Quilt Along. Quilter and fiber artist Emma Alcazar (Chickasaw) and artist, cultural educator, sewing instructor Nikki Corbett (Yup'ik) will discuss the inspiration behind their block patterns. The conversation will be moderated by Veruschka Zarate , quilt artist, international educator, and founder of Pride & Joy Quilting. This event will take place online via Zoom. Register now! Emma’s block pattern design responded to the theme of 20th century to present day (1902–2026). Download Emma's pattern to learn more. Nikki’s block pattern design responded to the theme of Our Shared Future (2026 and beyond). Download Nikki's pattern to learn more. About our speakers: Emma Alcazar (Chickasaw) is a Virginia-based quilter and fiber artist. Raised in Oklahoma, she holds a BA in Anthropology and MEd in Educational Leadership. After 18 years teaching English, she began focusing on creating art full time in 2022. She works with traditional quilting techniques, often incorporating Chickasaw or English language, to create hand-sewn art for display and use. Her quilts have appeared in multiple juried shows, including the Mid-Atlantic Quilt Festival, the Great Wisconsin Quilt Show, the Houston International Quilt Festival, and the Modern Quilt Guild’s QuiltCon; as well as at Exhibit C Gallery in Oklahoma City. Nikki Corbett is an artist, cultural educator, sewing instructor, wife, mother, and grandmother from Southwest Alaska, with family roots in Nunapitchuk and Bethel. She is the founder of Sew Yup'ik, a cultural arts initiative dedicated to revitalizing traditional Yup'ik sewing practices and passing knowledge to future generations. Her work centers on qaspeq (a hooded overshirt with large front pocket) making, nasqurrun (a Yup'ik woman’s dance headdress) revitalization, and traditional design elements that reflect ancestral teachings while engaging contemporary audiences. Her approach blends practical skill building with storytelling and emphasizes that Indigenous knowledge systems are living, evolving, and deeply relevant. Veruschka Zarate , the artist and designer behind Pride & Joy Quilting , is an award-winning quilt artist, pattern designer, international educator, and judge. Her quilts have been exhibited in museums and have earned some of the quilting industry’s highest honors including Best in Show at QuiltCon 2025, First Place in Piecing at QuiltCon, and QuiltCon People’s Choice. A proud firstborn daughter of a beautifully layered heritage, Veruschka’s roots span Puerto Rican, Cuban, Mexican, Irish, and French ancestry, along with Indigenous Taíno and Yaqui heritage. This rich intersection of cultures, histories, traditions, and stories has profoundly shaped the way she sees the world and continues to influence the artist, storyteller, teacher, and maker she has become. Images: Emma Alcazar, photo courtesy of Emma Alcazar; Nikki Corbett, photo by Jayme Huston Photography; Veruschka Zarate, photo courtesy of Veruschka Zarate. This project received funding from the Smithsonian’s “ Our Shared Future: 250 ,” a Smithsonian-wide initiative supported by private philanthropy and created to commemorate the nation’s 250th anniversary and advance the Smithsonian vision for the next 250 years.

events.name: NY | The Americas Film Festival New York: "Uiksaringitara (Wrong Husband)"
events.description: In 2000 BCE Igloolik, Nunavut, star-crossed teenage lovers Kaujak and Sapa are promised to each other since birth, but their bond is shattered when Kaujak’s father dies and her mother marries a man from a distant camp. The promise of a better future turns into a desperate struggle as Kaujak is besieged by aggressive suitors backed by a powerful, evil shaman. Despite the pressure, Kaujak holds fast to her heart, resisting all attempts to claim her and clinging to the hope that Sapa will return to make good on their childhood pledge. Director: Zacharias Kunuk (Inuk), Canada, 2025, 100 min., Inuktitut with English subtitles Content Advisory: contains scenes of physical violence. The Americas Film Festival New York (TAFFNY) is a film festival that showcases premieres, award winning films, and classic works about the cultures and peoples of the Americas. The festival is a project of the Division of Interdisciplinary Studies at the Center for Worker Education of City College of New York (The City University of New York - CUNY), in collaboration with the Cervantes Institute of NY and the Smithsonian's National Museum of the American Indian. events.name: Opening Celebration: Light Is a Plastic Medium
events.description: Celebrate the opening of Light Is a Plastic Medium: The Photography of Carlotta Corpron with a special evening suitable for visitors of all ages. Step inside our survey of work by the American abstract photographer and educator whose investigations into the poetics of light and form and innovative use of technology between the mid 1930s-1950s supported the establishment of photography as fine art. Learn more about Carlotta Corpron (1901-1988), her life and artistic achievements with talks by leading experts in the field including a return visit by Katy Hessel, art historian and founder of @thegreatwomenartists. Attendance will be limited and available on a first-come, first-served basis as gallery space allows. 6 pm: Curator Tour: Betsy Johnson 7 pm: Insights: Katy Hessel on Carlotta Corpron All galleries will be open. Circle back to some of our talked-about exhibitions: Big Things for Big Rooms Mark Bradford: Pickett’s Charge Laurie Anderson: Four Talks Adam Pendleton: Love, Queen Catch Revolutions: Art from the Hirshhorn Collection, 1860–1960 before it closes on Nov. 1. This exploration of the Museum’s extensive holdings received a final rotation. Discover masterworks by major figures like the American modernist painter Jacob Lawrence and contemporary abstractionist Lesley Vance and new acquisitions, including a striking sculpture by Thomas Houseago . Cap off the night by treating yourself to delicious refreshments for purchase from our partners at Dolcezza.

events.name: Center Stage
events.description: Director’s Cut, 35th Anniversary screening, in 4K Restoration! Watch the Trailer International superstar Maggie Cheung ( In the Mood for Love ) embodies tragic screen siren Ruan Lingyu in this unconventional biopic by Hong Kong New Wave master Stanley Kwan ( Rouge ). Known as the “Greta Garbo of China,“ Ruan was praised for her moving and emotive onscreen presence. But Ruan’s private life began to mirror the melodramas that brought her fame and was frequent fodder for the vicious Shanghai tabloids. This tumult culminated in her suicide at age 24. Kwan and Cheung paint a kaleidoscopic yet intimate portrait of the ill-fated actress, deftly blending lush period drama, archival footage, and metatextual documentary sequences of Cheung reflecting on Ruan’s legacy. The result is, much like the films of Ruan Lingyu themselves, “tender, vivid and almost overwhelmingly moving” ( Time Out ). Description adapted from Film Movement. Director: Stanley Kwan (Hong Kong). Released: 1991. Length: 154 min. Format: DCP. Language: Cantonese, Mandarin, and English with English subtitles. Presented by Fortune Star Media Limited, the restoration of the film was carried out from the original 35mm picture and optical soundtrack negative. The prints were repaired, cleaned, and scanned in Hong Kong, then digitally restored in 4K resolution in Bologna, Italy, by L’Immagine Ritrovata. Endorsed by the director, Stanley Kwan, the color correction was completed by Interface Video Production Ltd in Hong Kong. Copresented with JxJ – DC Jewish Film and Music which will also present two films on similar themes. Educational Partner: George Washington University Chinese Arts & Humanities Initiative . Image courtesy of Film Movement
